utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic to continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you. Examination by Tapuskovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, I have about 20 minutes more, and I'll try, if possible, to cover a few other things. Let me show you, but first can you please tell the Judges, after leaving Pretis on the 4th of April, 1992, during those years, subsequent years, did you ever go to the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did drop by, but not too many times. Only when I had time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Prosecution document 65 ter 02026.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you see this document? Take a look at who has issued and signed this document, and tell us out loud.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was issued by the secretariat for the economy of Vogosca municipality and it was signed by Milorad Motika, the manager of Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the next page, please. Do you see the title? Can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pretis production capacity."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please quickly take a look at the first page. Anyway, you know that I have shown this document to you before examination-in-chief and that you have seen it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these two -- what these first pages refer to, but please be brief.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first page, as well as other pages, concern the development of Pretis after the Second World War up to the 1990s, that is, the beginning of the war, and its production programme is shown over the period, including the civilian and military production.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what kind of industrial branch this was? What was the annual turnover and earnings from exports? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that for the time these were very high figures. They were expressed in dinars, but I cannot tell you exactly because I did not work in the financial department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is all written in this document. Can we please now look at the last page. And please pay attention to paragraph -- the fifth paragraph from the bottom. It begins with the word "Establish ..." Can you read this paragraph, and after that tell me whether this is consistent with the condition of the Pretis factory when you later came to visit it occasionally. Please read the paragraph which begins the words "Established."

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The sanctions imposed by Serbia on RS have had disastrous consequences on supplies of raw materials because the factory relies almost 100 per cent on supplies from SR Yugoslavia. It is even more difficult to procure tools, office supplies, and especially spare parts because most of the modern equipment is imported and it is difficult to import spare parts up to now."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the situation that you saw when you came to visit later, when these events happened in the period from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This situation prevailed throughout the war, as far as I was able to see when I visited the Pretis occasionally. But the situation deteriorated following the imposition of the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document, 65 ter 02026, be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document. Yesterday, you spoke about the events in Buca Potok, Zuc village, that happened in the first days, and how everything started in 1992. I'd like to show you now 65 ter document 03263. Mr. Kovacevic, please take a look at the title of this document, read it, and tell us what it pertains to, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Ministry of the Interior, and that's a daily report, number 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the date.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we don't have enough time to go through the entire document, could you please read the passage which begins -- that's the fourth paragraph, and it begins with "The enemy groups ..." Please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The enemy groups have attacked the village of Zuc from the position at Pofalici and Buca Potok. The attack was repelled and one of our combatants was wounded in this battle."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Without going into everything that is written here, does what you have just read correspond to what you said and how you described the events at the beginning and what you said yesterday during the examination-in-chief relating to Buca Potok and Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely the reflection of that. Only the name of Milojica Stevanovic, the victim was not mentioned here. Everything else is here. I mentioned Zivkovic, Odzakovic, Stevanovic, Rakic, and other families who moved out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the document 0263 be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D228, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, since I have very little time left, you described the events that took place towards the end of 1994. Can you tell us very briefly, what was the situation between December and May? You told us a few things, but can you tell us briefly a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between December 1994 and May 1995, I said that I think that a truce was signed, although I'm not sure. There were no war operations and activities either by the BH army or by our side. Therefore, this truce was being observed until the end of May, approximately, when provocations started and then later became an offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us briefly what happened when this offensive was mounted? Can you please tell the Chamber that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The BH army mounted an offensive on all points in Nisici, towards Hadzici, Treskovica, our front line. I'm talking about the battlefield of Rajlovac and Zuc where I was, including Ilidza as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the Rajlovac battlefield. Up until then, you were threatened from which positions during the whole war? I'm talking about the positions where you were.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, from the direction of Zuc, the Zuc plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when the offensive started, were you threatened from other directions as well? You mentioned Hadzici; you mentioned Nisici. Were there any other attacks that you expected to come not only from Zuc but from other directions as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the area of responsibility that we covered was actually covered by my brigade - excuse me - included the Nisici front, at the time we were attacked from two sides and there was also fire coming from Igman during the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of all that and these attacks, I'm going to show you Defence document D159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have that brought up on the screens. D159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at who issued that report, what the date was, and read out loud paragraph number 1. Can you tell me whether that tallies with the events as you remembered them in the time you refer to and concerning the things you've described? Please read it out loud, the heading, the date, and item 1.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on active combat actions by the command of the 1st Corps - interpreter's correction - command of the 12th Division. The date, the 4th of July, 1995, signed by the commander of the 12th Brigade, Brigadier Fikret Prevljak. Item 1 states literally: "During the period between the 15th of June and the 3rd of July, 1995, we fired from all types of weaponry that we had at our disposal against over 300 VTs of the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that correspond to what you actually were able to observe at the positions where you were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I intentionally paused here when weaponry was mentioned and pieces as well, because in our language these are two different terms. When I say "weaponry" or "weapons," I mean infantry weapons, and "pieces" pertains to artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the period of the clashes and in the period referred to here, can you tell us, first of all, how many soldiers from your platoon and from your positions were killed? And, in particular, do you know anything of any casualties among the civilians of Pofalici and other locations? Can you tell us something about that or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally know of a soldier who was killed on that line by the name of Radoslav Miskovic. I know that there were some wounded soldiers. I remember two of them. And there were many other things, although I didn't keep track. I cannot tell you precisely, but I know that Dragan Krnjajic was wounded at our position as well as Mirko Tambur, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about civilians. Well, there was one civilian who was killed in front of his house in my settlement by the name of Mirko Micukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And to conclude with, can you tell me whether you had contacts with the population during this period? Did you have any contacts with refugees, and do you know what their feelings were at the time and how they felt? That would also be my last question.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, to correct the transcript, it isn't Mirko Miskovic but Mirko Micukic. And concerning your last question, the refugees had already gone through the atrocities at Pofalici and other locations at Sarajevo, but the offensive that year took place throughout the territory of Republika Srpska. And since the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was far more numerous than ours, people were expecting loss of territory, extermination, persecution. However, at Pofalici it did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said the Bosnia-Herzegovina army was far more numerous than yours. Can you tell us something about the relative level of weaponry as between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you much. I can only tell you what I presumed since I'm not an expert in those matters. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over the barracks, as I mentioned yesterday, from the JNA. I think it has also been recorded in the broadcast when the JNA was trying to pull out and to save their skins, and they just moved into their barracks. They were not inferior to us in any way. At least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Ms. Edgerton. May I inquire whether you wish to have that last document exhibited? That's to Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this already is an exhibit. This is D159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, as you've heard, my name is Carolyn Edgerton and I'm going to be asking you some questions from the Prosecution bench about some of the evidence that you've given today and some other matters, and I just wanted to tell you, if you find my questions unclear at any time or in any way, please tell me and I'll be happy to rephrase them or try and clarify them for you. Is that all right? Now, yesterday, you spoke a little bit about your military service record and said that you were a platoon commander and your company commander was Sinisa Krsman, but I noticed that was, unless I was mistaken, from 1993. Yesterday, you spoke about the formation of the military unit you were a part of in May 1992, and I'd actually like to go back to that, if that's all right. Now, you mentioned earlier that in the context of the agreement over the evacuation and surrender of the -- evacuation of the JNA and surrender of the JNA barracks in Sarajevo - Marsal Tito, Jusuf Dzonlic, Viktor Bubanj - people in your neighbourhood started organising themselves under the Territorial Defence Staff, and you said: "So we set up units. Rather, the TO staff organised units, armed fighters using the weapons left over after the JNA had evacuated the Rajlovac barracks." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please say yes or no rather than nod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to suggest to you that the evacuation of the barracks you mentioned or you named actually took place at the very end of May 1992 and the organisation of the Serbian people in the area of Rajlovac began much earlier than that date, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, the date of the army's withdrawal from the Rajlovac barracks, as I specified yesterday, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I was to say to you that the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac was proclaimed on February 23rd of 1992, prior to the referendum on independence and prior to the recognition of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of April, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to repeat that I don't know that date either, and I don't see any reason to. It's a matter of the local authorities for each municipality, the way the local communes and municipalities were organised. As for the exact date when the Serb municipality of Rajlovac was founded, that I don't know. I know that it was sometime in early 1992, but not the date. And it's a local authority matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're familiar with Radovan Karadzic, who was the President of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I take it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He was a media figure over the course of many years, so I imagine you would have heard his voice many times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. That being the case, I'd like us to listen to an intercepted conversation, which is -- the transcript of which is going to appear on the screen in front of you so that you can follow in your own language, and it's number 03232. The date of that conversation is 23 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kovacevic, do you recognise the voice of Radovan Karadzic in that conversation? I'm sorry, the transcript doesn't record nods.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure. I can guess or try to recognise, but I cannot be certain. You also have to allow for a possibility that it's not him. If I'm to be held responsible and held to my word, I would never say for sure that this was indeed he, not even after listening to this. As for me to be able to say whether it is he or not, I can't remember some other even more familiar voices, let alone President Karadzic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This conversation mentioned the place Reljevo. Where is Reljevo, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reljevo is a local commune in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the two men in this conversation, Karadzic and Mr. Grkovic, as you saw, talked about the boundaries of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac, going as far south as the TV station and going north to Vogosca and going to the west to Osijek. Does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I don't understand how you can put that to the witness, the two men in this conversation, Karadzic and whoever the other one was, because he hasn't agreed that it is Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was simply saying that on the basis of those recorded in the transcript that you saw before you, Your Honours, but, yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the two people in this conversation talked about the territorial definition of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac, as I said before, as far south as the TV station, as far north as Vogosca, and as far east as -- pardon me, west as Osijek. Would you agree that that corresponds with your knowledge of the territorial boundaries of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain that things are that way exactly, but if this is an authentic conversation, then I guess so. I wasn't privy to that. I didn't have a map of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac. I wasn't into that, and I don't know what these two men may have discussed, Mr. Grkovic and President Karadzic. Therefore, I don't know. As for any maps of the municipality of Rajlovac, I did see it at some point, but I don't think it was exactly as it was portrayed here. I think it was smaller. It was shown on TV. Although the northern and western borders do tally more or less. Again, I have to tell you that I had nothing to do with politics. I don't know what was being decided at the sessions of the local Municipal Assembly and so on and so forth. As for the map, I told you what I think of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So based on your answer, what I take from your answer is that although to your knowledge, to your personal knowledge, the borders of the municipality may have been slightly smaller, the northern and western borders corresponded more or less with this conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be entered as a Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P769, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Tapuskovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this has already been exhibited, but I object on the basis of principle. As regards any future intercepts, if a witness can say something about those for certain, then I have nothing against your ruling. But, in principle, if he's uncertain whether it is as the Prosecutor puts it, then he cannot say anything and he cannot be held responsible. Therefore, maybe such intercepts should be introduced via some other witnesses. Your ruling stands as it is, but such intercepts may come again, and I'd ask you to ask the Prosecutor to introduce such intercepts only through witnesses which can actually confirm those. That is my general position as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I admitted it on the basis of his agreement with the Prosecution's proposition that the borders identified in the municipality, identified in the conversation that he heard, correspond with the -- are more or less correct. So I admitted it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now ask we see the document with the 65 ter number 03256 on the screen, which are the notes of a commemorative speech on the promulgation of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac recovered following the reintegration in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you see the document in your language in front of you? Mr. Kovacevic, could I draw your attention to the first sentence on the first page, which reads: "We gathered on 23 February 1992 and promulgated the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac." Does your memory, Mr. Kovacevic, now stand refreshed as to when the Serb municipality of Rajlovac was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? As I said a minute ago, the 23rd of February was crossed out here and then written again, which may be correct and then it may not be. However, I didn't take part in it, and I don't know. The newly appointed municipal president took part in that, as well as some deputies and delegates, whatever they were called at the time. I was just a plain ordinary citizen. I took no part in the formation of that Serb municipality of Rajlovac or its promulgation; therefore, I cannot tell you much about it. The date seems to be inserted later. It needn't -- it doesn't have to mean that it's incorrect, but I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, who was the author of this? Who held the speech, and what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The occasion, Your Honour, as set out in greater detail in the document itself, was a commemorative gathering on the promulgation of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, and the Prosecution's submission, given the location of recovery of the document, which was from the office of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac following the reintegration, was that it was written by a member of the Serbian municipality assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So was the speech ever held?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, is your question perhaps more whether or not the gathering ever took place? Certainly, the affair, in the Prosecution's submission, was commemorated, but we've not had evidence in this court at this time to this effect. The evidence has been brought before other Trial Chambers in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we're looking at a document. We don't know who the author is. We're not sure if it was ever read out. We're not sure if the occasion took place. So what are we exactly to believe here?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, I would like to put certain passages of this document to the witness to see whether they correspond with the witness's recollection of what took it place in the period leading up to May 1992 when he's spoken about the formation of his territorial units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour Judge Harhoff, I would like to hear the Prosecutor's response to your question. I think it is very important to know who authored this document. It is very important for the continuation of the cross-examination with this witness. Perhaps we should show the witness the last page of this speech and then he might be able to tell us who drafted that. And this is very necessary for us to be able to do anything with this document that might be exhibited. Perhaps we can look at the last page to see whether we can tell who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, to whom is it written?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see the addressees, "Dear Gentlemen and Dear Guests," Your Honours, at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's notes on the speech for the commemoration of the promulgation of the Serb municipality of Rajlovac. Regardless of who may have written the document or who it may have been addressed to, Your Honours, I'd submit I'm certainly entitled to put propositions, factual propositions as set out in this document, to the witness to determine whether or not they correspond with his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't know to whom it is written or who wrote it. I believe its reliability may be in question. Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll allow you to put the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, if I could direct you to page 5 of the B/C/S translation, paragraph 4; on the English, page 6. It reads -- perhaps we could scroll the B/C/S version upwards a little bit just to make sure everything -- it reads: "Thanks to politically tactic activities, we managed to take over the most important military and civilian facilities --"

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Start again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear me now at all?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The page on the original has to be scrolled down, not up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph, I think, 4 on this page, it reads: "Thanks to politically tactic activities, we managed to take over the most important military and civilian facilities in Rajlovac, even though some of them had well-organised units the Territorial Defence." Mr. Kovacevic, have you heard the passage I've just read to you and do you see it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said a few moments ago I have no idea who wrote this, and I do not see any reason why I should agree or disagree with this because I never participated in this. At that time I was a citizen who went to work in Belgrade in 1992 every day. If this is from February 1992, I mean, a document from February 1992, which is questionable. I went to work regularly at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, all of a sudden we see Belgrade. Nobody mentioned Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is what we heard the witness say. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he did. I heard him say Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You speak B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Understand B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- some B/C/S, and I can hear what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good for you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've been here a long time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe you can assist the Defence team at times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That may be my future one of these days, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, what we were focusing on was what you had testified yesterday where you said: "The TO staff organised units, armed fighters, using the weapons left over after the JNA had evacuated the Rajlovac barracks," and what I'm asking you is whether, in light of what you testified yesterday, the proposition that you managed to "take over the most important military and civilian facilities in Rajlovac, even though some of them had well-organised units of the Territorial Defence," was correct. Are you prepared to agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I spoke about the organisation of units when I was involved in those units. That certainly is not this date that is here in this document, and I cannot agree with this because I don't know about this. I only know about the time that I referred to yesterday, when I was involved in the organisation of units under the Territorial Defence. Now, whether they had activities before that or not, again I'm telling you at the time that this document is dated I went to work regularly for about two months. Not only me, but all of the town of Sarajevo went regularly to work, to their factories. As for these activities, I have no comment to make. I have nothing to add, nothing to deny --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, you can't take this any further, this issue any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And since this was a matter which went solely to the witness's credibility, I won't be seeking to tender the document at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could move, Mr. Kovacevic, to what you've spoken about again, the time when you were involved in the organisation of units under the Territorial Defence. Could you tell me, was the Rajlovac Territorial Defence ever subordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in May 1992, which is the time you specifically addressed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday the Territorial Defence, as it was called then, although the Territorial Defence was already divided. Every municipality had its Territorial Defence, and every local commune made some kind of units at that time of the first conflicts. In May 1992, I said yesterday, the army of Republika Srpska was created in the beginning of May, sometime around the 10th. So I, as an ordinary soldier, could not know who was my superior, who was my subordinate, except for my immediate superiors. But probably, by virtue of the fact that the army of Republika Srpska was established, these units in Rajlovac were probably subordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, could we see document 03234, please. Pardon me, 03244. My apologies. 03244.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down in the B/C/S version slowly and then go to the second page so the witness can see the entire document. In fact, go to the second page when he says he's had a chance to read the provisions of the document.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What should I read on this document, what paragraph, or should I read the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's not a long document, Mr. Kovacevic, and you're entitled to have a look at the document, but I would ask you to pay particular attention to paragraph (e), please. Sorry, in your version, paragraph (e).

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours, that there seems to be an error in the paragraph numbering of the English translation. I'll have that corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you read paragraph (e), Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's rather illegible. I guess that you're interested in the bit that starts with "The Rajlovac Brigade ..." If so, I'm going to read that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, please, of the document so the witness can see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you see the signature of the gentleman who was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at that time, Tomislav Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kovacevic, here on the 22nd of May, 1992, you see an order from General Sipcic restructuring, effectively, the territorial forces of the Serb republic to form larger units. Now, to the best of your knowledge, is this order consistent with the situation as you recalled it at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, as for what I know -- and I'd like to emphasise once again that at that time I was an ordinary soldier who was at the line underneath Zuc plateau. So this is the first time I hear of this. Actually, perhaps I did hear of it, but I forgot who the first commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. At that time, I didn't know that. Today neither.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the question by going back to my original -- to something you said originally.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your testimony earlier this morning, you said that you thought the Rajlovac Territorial Defence was by this time subordinated to the SRK. Do you have any reason to change that position now, seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territorial unit of Rajlovac under the jurisdiction of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at that time, in May? I mean, I said I think that if the army of Republika Srpska had already been established, that all units the Territorial Defence were linked up within the system of the army of Republika Srpska. That's what I think. I'm not sure. I was not in such a high position to be able to know that, the date, the beginning, or -- I mean, maybe even up to the month of June they were not linked up, or maybe they were but I didn't know about it. I said I think, because the army was established on the 12th. According to this system of automatism, all the units of Republika Srpska should be linked up into a whole. Again, I say "I think." I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm not sure I quite understand. Are you actually disputing the veracity of this document, even though it effectively goes to confirm what you testified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not disputing the veracity of this document. I'm just saying that I don't know of this document. It is probably true. I mean, I cannot confirm it as true, except for what I said. I claim that the truth is what I said, and I'm not withdrawing in terms of what I said. And if that corresponds with the document that is in front of me, then, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honour, I'd like to ask that this be tendered as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P770, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was the Rajlovac Territorial Defence eventually subsumed into the Rajlovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you, probably yes. If it goes without saying that every military unit has to be linked up, then yes. But I don't know. I was not an officer or a signatory of some documents. I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know where the brigade headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade headquarters was at the Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recall who the brigade commander was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first commander of the brigade, I remember the last name. I don't remember his first name. Vujasin, Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have one further document from 1992, and at that point I'll leave that here, and the document bears the ter number 03248.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, what you should see on the screen in front of you is an SRK command order dated 7 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of the document, please. Flip over that way so the witness could see the signature. On the B/C/S, please. I don't see that that's the last page of the B/C/S document. It doesn't correspond with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Prosecutor's list, yes, I got this document. I saw it, I read it, but it ends precisely on this page that we saw just now, and there is no signature on that page, and I didn't see whether the document had a signature somewhere else. I did not receive any such thing. On this page there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see we have an e-court error. Obviously all pages of the B/C/S version haven't been uploaded, and unless we can find it very quickly, to save time, I'll move on and come back to that one part of 1992, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then moving on, in fact jumping to 1993, Mr. Kovacevic. Your unit, I understand, was subsumed, or the Rajlovac Brigade, which included your unit, was subsumed under the control of the Vogosca Tactical Group which later became the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And where was the command headquarters of the Vogosca Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the Motel Sonja. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber where the Motel Sonja was so that they know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the condition that it is correct what I said, namely, that this is at the Sonja Motel, not Sanja, it is between Rajlovac and Vogosca by an intersection on the road. Krivoglavci is the name of the settlement. Again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again what, Mr. Kovacevic? I'm sorry, you said something that the interpreter translated to me. No?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "again"; he said "opet."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, from this time, the time at which your unit was incorporated into the Vogosca Tactical Group, up until the end of the war, did you, Mr. Kovacevic, have any direct contact whatsoever with SRK command staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had meetings in my company with the company commander, sometimes with the battalion commander, commander of the battalion. I personally never took part in some meetings - well, let's put it this way - at a higher level. I mean, I am referring to the corps command, the brigade command. I had no such opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So have you ever, during the course of the indictment period from August 1994 until the end of the war, met Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, no. I met him through the media. The general did come, but I did not have an opportunity to see him. He came to the area of responsibility of my brigade, but I personally did not have an opportunity to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know that he came to the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember this occasion. I think it was some celebration in Vogosca. I remember that they said that the general would come to that celebration, and I was at the lines then so I could not attend and I could not see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that might have been? Was it in 1994 or 1995 or actually sometime prior to that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. The end of 1994, I think, or the beginning of 1995. I think it was cold. That's why I'm saying the end or the beginning, because it was winter, I think. That is how I remember it, that the weather was cold on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, do you remember on what occasions you saw him on the media?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media -- well, usually I could see not only General Milosevic but, generally speaking -- well, not media. I mean officers of the Serb army and civilian authorities. I could see when there were some celebrations, when some things that were important happened at the front line. But for the most part, when enemy offensives were under way, the general, well, would issue statements and things like that for the people and for the army. Of course, for the army commands went in different ways, but for the people, well, at meetings I could see that on the news, the daily news, very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I understand that the last page of the document we just recently dealt with has been uploaded into e-court, so perhaps we could go back to 03248. That's the last page, according to the translation. Now we have the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Kovacevic, that this represents an order signed by Tomislav Sipcic, again, commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at that time, 7 June 1992, and the document is directed -- the order is directed to, among others, the Rajlovac Brigade. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1, please. I see the pagination is different. In the English version, could we go to page 2, because we'd like to see paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, if I could direct your attention to paragraph 2, it says: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps has a task to," and the word in your language is "ocistiti," "parts of Sarajevo where the Serbian population is in majority by functional deployment of forces; if possible, to divide the town along the line Nedzarici-Stup-Rajlovac; to secure the area of Sarajevo airport and its surroundings to "izvrsiti ciscenje," Mojmilo, Dobrinja, Butmir, and Sokolovic Kolonija." Do you see that, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move down to paragraph 4 in both versions, and for the relevant paragraph, you'll have to go to the next page in the -- the relevant sentence, you'll have to go to the next page in the English, and the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Kovacevic, would you agree that SRK forces have been ordered to divide the city of Sarajevo along the line Nedzarici-Stup-Rajlovac and, by further activities, take over dominant facilities? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the order-issuing authority meant, although I have read the broader context, not only what you read. And then there's also the blockade of the Zlastiste-Pale road, then of the Trnovo-Lukavice road. So I don't see exactly what was meant, cutting the town into sections or taking over this from a strategic point of view. I'm telling you again, I'm not very knowledgeable about this. I was an ordinary soldier. I don't know what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I am intervening only when things are very, very important, and in this case, what is concerning -- what's interesting here is that on page 27, line 15, we can see "Pale road," and in B/C/S the witness said "deblokada puta Zlatiste-Pale," and the English interpretation said "deblockade." The LiveNote will certainly be corrected accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move further in this document down to paragraph 5.6, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm receiving French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I think you're also knowledgeable in French.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Much more so than in B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.6 sets out, Mr. Kovacevic, specific tasks of the Rajlovac Brigade, "to persistently hold the achieved line," and further in 5.7, "to persistently defend achieved positions and prepare some forces to be ready to intervene in the area north of Rajlovac and to be active in the direction of Rajlovac-Stup in the town-dividing phase." Would you agree that's what the document says in those paragraphs, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what this undoubtedly says, but it's not for me to agree because I don't know. Generally speaking, this is the first time I see this document. I mean, I didn't even know about this document ever until now. And I said yesterday at this same time I was wounded at this line when there was this BH army attack at Zuc on the 8th of June. So I'm a bit confused by this, but no problem, I'll find my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the BiH army attack was -- offensive that you've described was one day following the issuance of this order; is that correct? This order to the SRK to work for the division of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct, that it was one day following the date of this order but in my zone of responsibility, that is to say, the zone of responsibility of the Rajlovac Brigade. I don't know exactly whether it started earlier on at some other axes, Ilijas, Lukavica, Hadzici. At any rate, in my zone of responsibility of the Rajlovac Brigade, the offensive started exactly on the 8th of June, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, on the basis of this rather strongly worded order that's directed to all other brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, including yours, I put it to you that the Rajlovac Brigade wasn't just standing in front of their homes, as you had said yesterday, not only defending their territory but defending territory they had achieved with a view to securing the division of Sarajevo. What would you say to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said yesterday. These lines that, as you say, were captured, they were set up there without any conflict. There was no seizure. They were in front of our houses. Here in the hotel, I have a document that can substantiate and confirm that this is where my house was and where the line was. Even UNPROFOR drew these lines in that way. It is true that we were precisely in front of our houses, at least I know that. And I can show you again on the same map which villages and neighbourhoods were involved. These were all Serbian villages, and you can verify that in a hundred ways. These were the Serbian houses, and the line ran by the houses. In this area, which, according to you, the Rajlovac Brigade occupied or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it was not at all, let's say, populated by other ethnicities. We didn't capture anything. These were our property, our land, our forests which we owned, and this is where the line was set up at the beginning of the war. We were attacked, as I told you, on the morning of the 8th of June in those places. We didn't attack, seize, or divide the town as you are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I'd just like to follow up on something you said, Mr. Kovacevic, because it reflects a theme I heard from you yesterday as well. You said just now: "... in this area, which, according to you, the Rajlovac Brigade occupied or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, was not at all, let's say, populated by other ethnicities." Mr. Kovacevic, I put to you that in fact the area occupied by the Rajlovac Brigade and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was in fact densely populated by other ethnicities to the point where ethnicities were living -- mixed ethnicities were living in apartment buildings together. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that in the area, in this area that was under the control of the SRK, that there were no members of other ethnic groups. Yesterday, I said that only about the area of the Rajlovac Brigade. Now, in response to your question, in the area of the Rajlovac Brigade and its zone of responsibility, I think that the ratio was 97 per cent Serbs and 3 per cent others. And there were no apartment buildings, because these neighbourhoods mainly consist of private houses. I'm telling you again, I cannot be very decisive about the exact percentage, but I think between 95 and 97 per cent were Serbs and the rest accounted for 3 to 5 per cent. I don't know about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I never said anything in that sense yesterday. I was talking about the area of responsibility of the Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something missing in the transcript. On page 30, line 18, after the witness said [In English] "... consist of private houses," [Interpretation] the witness added, and I'll say it in B/C/S, "iskljucivo," and then he said exclusively, and then not exclusively, but was only made up of private houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. What was omitted after "private houses"? May I have that? You can say it in B/C/S so I can have it translated, what you claim to have --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it would be perhaps safer to ask -- to put the question to the witness just to see what kind of houses were in those villages. He talked about private houses. He did not talk about apartment buildings. So there were no apartment buildings there, but the witness just stated that there were private houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, can you just tell us what you said? Tell us what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want a long narration, just in relation to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I said: Exclusively private houses with no apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was the neighbourhood consisting of private homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you refute the Prosecutor's suggestion that it was an area, I believe the Prosecutor said, with mixed ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one part, yes, as I said, this very low percentage, not a mixed one. How shall I put it? In one area there were a few members of other ethnicities, whereas the other part was completely of the same ethnical composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Kovacevic, what you said yesterday was there were no Muslims residing within a 20-kilometre radius. In fact, 20 kilometres is an incredibly far distance and spans the width of the city of Sarajevo. Let's go back, Witness, to members of other ethnic groups in the area of the Rajlovac Brigade, and perhaps we can talk about that in the context of the area of responsibility of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to hear from the Defence counsel. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, the Prosecutor put forward a thesis and the comment of what she found in his statement. I think the witness should be allowed to respond to this, whether he actually said that there were no Muslims within the 20-kilometre radius. I'd like to hear the witness's answer to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are correct, yes. That was the question you put to the witness and he hasn't answered it. The question was that yesterday you said that there were no Muslims residing within a 20-kilometre radius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is correct or whether I said that the majority population was Serbian in the area of 20 kilometres, so the majority. So this more or less is equal to the area of the Rajlovac Brigade. Let me explain. This is an area stretching from Ilidza and Ilijas, Sarajevo Polje, next to the River Bosna. And let me go back to the same thing that I said, that there were 6 to 7 per cent other ethnic groups and the rest were Serbs. And this is what I think I said yesterday when I spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, this is absolutely something that the Prosecutor is entitled to seek an explanation to, but please, we have to be consistent. What the Defence is always asked to do is to quote exactly and precisely from the transcript what the witness said without asking the witness to explain his words. There is to doubt that the Prosecutor is entitled to put these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have chapter, verse, and page, Ms. Edgerton? I hope we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope so, too, Your Honours. I will in a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do that in the break, because we are past the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. I'd like us to try to move away from this business of, You said this and you said that and it's in the transcript. Let us see whether we can get on with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking before we broke about the area of responsibility of your brigade, and I'd like to ask you the following: Did the area of responsibility of your brigade include the town of Vogosca? It included the town of Vogosca, didn't it? And that's -- a yes or no answer would suffice for that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything, and I will answer you in this way: Probably, yes, but I cannot confirm that because I don't know anything about the lines and the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did the area --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand properly. Now I understand the question. The Rajlovac Brigade did not include Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It included the village of Semizovac, didn't it, and the village of Svraka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Semizovac neither.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the village of Svraka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither Svraka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The village of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The village of Dobrosevici?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's the next village.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The area of Otes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's focus on Dobrosevici and Ahatovici. No Muslims lived in those villages from 1994 through to 1995, did they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These were in the area of responsibility of your brigade. They didn't live in those villages because they were killed or expelled in 1992; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim what happened with them, whether they were killed or expelled. What I know, and I'm telling you again, I wasn't either in Dobrosevici or in Ahatovici. I was on Zuc. And in my area of responsibility, as far as I know, there were conflicts in Dobrosevici and Ahatovici between the forces of the army of Republika Srpska and the Green Berets or the Territorial Defence, as it was called then, so in those villages. What happened after that, whether they were killed or expelled, I have no knowledge about that because I didn't take part either in those clashes, nor did I learn later any particulars about these events, in the aftermath. The area of responsibility, yes. The units deployed in this area took part in the conflicts. My unit did not take part in the conflict. Therefore, I don't know whether they were expelled or killed as you put it so decisively. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Three words would have sufficed as an answer to that question, and you would have made yourself equally clear, with respect, Mr. Kovacevic. But now I'd like to move on to one last period remaining in 1992, and I want to talk about the incident you spoke of at the Pretis factory in 1992 relating to what you say were the takeover of weapons. You didn't see it, did you? You didn't see it, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. It wasn't the weapons. It was ammunition, the takeover of ammunition from the Pretis factory, because there was no weapons in Pretis. It is true. I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you weren't there, were you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't know what, if anything, was taken because you've only heard about it or seen stories about it on TV. So you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said how I learnt about this, whether something was taken or what was taken, and I learnt about that from the security guards from the factory who, a day or two after the attack because I don't remember when I first went to the factory after the attack, described to me how this attack happened. Now, 10 or 15 years later, we are constantly hearing about this attack and the takeover of ammunition from Pretis. I didn't need to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you must speak more slowly in the interests of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Witness, because you're from the area with the name of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And precisely because of the pace of his speech, the transcript didn't record that he has been listening for months how Vikic is boasting nowadays on TV what he had taken from Pretis in those times. Mr. Vikic can be seen very often on television in the present time, and this was not recorded in the transcript because he was speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let the witness just tell us that again so we can have it from the witness, and at a reasonable pace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat what happened on that day, or shall I repeat how I saw Vikic several times on television boasting about this action?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just the latter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the recent years, at least three times I saw Vikic in the programmes on the state television bragging about this action of taking over the ammunition from the Pretis factory, and he claimed that by so doing they defended the city, because they took large quantities of anti-tank Osa 2 rockets. According to what he's saying in these shows, that prevented a tank and armoured attack on Sarajevo. This is what I've seen several times in the last few years.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Anything you know about this incident you've heard from other sources. That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but from the participants in the events --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those directly involved in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe it's time for us to hear from another participant in the events, the Serb leader who actually organised the Serbs in their response to the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like us to play a video-clip now of Jovan Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Jovan Tintor was a very influential figure in Vogosca and Rajlovac areas, wasn't he? He's a Serb whose name was known throughout the municipality.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Known, yes, but I don't see why he would be influential. He was not either a civilian or a military official, at least not in my municipality. Neither a military or a civilian official. But I know that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He was a member and head of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Serbian municipality of Vogosca was the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. I was in Rajlovac, I was in the Rajlovac Brigade, and I -- it is true I worked in Pretis, which is in Vogosca, and I completed my employment on the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could see the video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, now having seen Mr. Tintor, who was the leader of the Serbs, inside that factory and having heard him say, "Thanks to our presence of mind, thanks to our security, we succeeded in defending the factory and we put it to an end," does that change your view as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that there is some discrepancy there; therefore, I'm not changing my view. What Mr. Tintor is saying is what I said yesterday, that only in the third attempt of their breaking in it happened that they thwarted that. There were people wounded. He mentioned that there were people killed; I don't know about that. Dragan Vikic never mentioned sustaining any casualties, wounded or killed. Dragan Vikic is not mentioning that. Tintor is talking about the third attempt, and those were the Green Berets or territorials from Kobilja Glava who wanted to take this opportunity, just as the special unit took the opportunity, to get hold of part of those weapons -- I mean not weapons, ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in that third attempt, this is what happened according to what Mr. Tintor was saying. As far as I know, and I also spoke about security guards who were tied in and these were my colleagues with whom I had been working for 10 years, two times the special units pulled it out and the Green Berets started to attack from Kobilja Glava, and that is when they organised themselves and the clashes broke out and ended with people getting wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, so what you're saying is, on the basis of your secondhand knowledge, you're prepared to dispute what one of the organisers of the incident said, what one of the Serb leaders of the incident said; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dispute the part for which I claim to have heard about from Dragan Vikic. He never mentioned this clash.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. 03267, please. And, yes, could I ask this video be tendered as the next Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was 03267.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, you see in front of you from June 12, 1992, a report from the Ministry of Economy of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which says in the very first line: "From the moment the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Pretis factory ... has remained undamaged. There were some minor misappropriations of materials, tools, kits, machine parts, vehicles and the like." Now, looking at this document and having heard Mr. Tintor and his version of what happened, are you still sticking to your story, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what the source of my information was, and I stand by what I saw personally on TV. This is not my story.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document entered as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't know what the date is, nor do we know who signed this document. We cannot see anything on this document. No, there is no date. I think we have received this document, but we cannot see either the date or the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we be directed to the date and the signature, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've just provided the date, which was the 12th of June, 1992. And the signature, if we could go to the second page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no signature on the document. We don't know what the nature of the document is; therefore, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, is it on your list of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was on the revised list which was -- it was on the revised list which was finalised this morning and sent out to Defence counsel yesterday evening, Your Honours. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the heading again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not receive this last night.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the parties were all forwarded these on the e-mail, including the Trial Chamber. I have to admit, it was 7.11 p.m., after -- that was the time of the e-mail yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, what did the witness say in relation to the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the face of the witness's testimony that he heard secondhand through the media that some -- either ammunition or explosives for ammunition were taken, substantial quantities according to the media, I put the first and second sentence in this document to him which said in fact there were minor misappropriations of materials, tool kits, machine parts, vehicles and the like, to see if, having heard Mr. Tintor and looking at this document which I would submit, Your Honours, has all the indicia of reliability, he still held to the story that he had heard in the media. And his reply was he sticks to what he heard in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has not agreed with your proposition or what is represented in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He has not agreed with what is represented in the document, which is -- which purports to be and seems to be a report to the Ministry of the Economy on the situation in Pretis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll not admit the document. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm informed by my colleague Ms. Bosnjakovic, I omitted to tender ter number 03248, which we dealt with earlier. Yes. If it could be tendered. I would like to tender it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit that one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P772.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, just one question for clarification to the witness. Witness, as of the 4th of April, 1992, right up until the end of the war, who was in control of the Pretis factory? Was it the ABiH or was it the SRK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Pretis factory was controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Two more brief areas of questioning, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you were never inside the confrontation lines in Bosnian-held territory of Sarajevo during the course of the war, were you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So never being inside, you never saw what the MUP did or might have done, whether or not they were taking part in combat, on the inside of the confrontation lines, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that I know what the MUP was doing inside the confrontation line, but what I said was that we used to encounter them at the confrontation line or the lines of separation. And there was an instance when we killed one of them wearing a special police uniform. It was at Zuc. Therefore, I know they participated in combat. I never said I knew what they were doing within the territory that was controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whether they directed the traffic or whether they were on patrols, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your statement that they participated in combat throughout the war was based on this one single incident now that you've just spoken about; isn't that correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the one that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just one final question. Never having been inside the confrontation lines during the course of the war, you never -- you were never in a position to personally experience privations that the civilians of Sarajevo might have been subject to, that being no water, no gas, and no electricity; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for gas, electricity, and water, just so that you know, it was it all interconnected. It was the same system. It wasn't -- it wasn't possible for a part of Sarajevo or Rajlovac or Hadzici to have gas and water supply and Sarajevo, or, rather, its centre would not. Therefore, whenever we had water, electricity, and gas, they did, too. Therefore, your question is pointless, the question about the privations of those inside the city. We had the same problems they did; civilians, I mean. The same problems that existed in Sarajevo were on our side as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, with respect, I know almost exactly how the fuel and infrastructure was interconnected. My question to you was: Never having been inside the confrontation lines, you have no personal experience of the privations civilians inside those lines suffered, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have a point, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, an objection, since there was something in the transcript that we disagree with. The Prosecutor was testifying. She said, "I know." A Prosecutor may not testify. She said she knew and then she asked the witness to confirm that. I don't think it is a proper way to question a witness. One cannot say, "I know this and that." Of course she can offer reference or proof of what she's saying, but she may not say, "I know" and then ask the witness to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No importance is to be attached to that statement. Do you have another question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's the cross-examination. I have no other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, speaking about the production of the Pretis factory --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.
