So we're speaking about the production of the Pretis factory, and you stated that there were mines, ammunition, explosives, Osa missiles, and also aerial bombs, air bombs that were manufactured and stored in the sheds or stores. On the 4th of April when you ended your professional activities, you said that there were air bombs also in those sheds. Can you confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I knew of everything that was there. I said that those were the things that we used to produce and what could be found in the warehouses. At the moment of my leaving, I didn't know exactly what the inventory was. Out of the entire line of production, I guess a number of such items and types of product were stored there. I didn't say exactly what and how many, though. It should have been there, I guess, because the production went on until that very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You may know how the air -- do you know how the air bombs were used? Can you say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I saw some aircraft bombs in the factory. As far as I know, they can only be used in aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So according to you, the items were stolen by the special MUP forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and according to the Prosecutor, those items stayed within the premises of the factory. But from what you experienced as a former employee of the factory but also as a military, would you have learned anything as to the use of such bombs, of the air bombs, by the ABiH or by the SRK after the theft was done?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. I don't know. As I said, I was an infantry soldier in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is, Your Honours, concerning the two documents exhibited by the Prosecutor. But let us start first with P772. Perhaps the witness can have a look at the last page of that document that we saw a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in item 6, can you read it out loud for the Chamber, the second paragraph of item 6?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I strictly forbid mistreating civilian unarmed population. As for the prisoners of war, they should be treated in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions. What we approve is the use of one BK," which is a combat kit of ammunition, "and 1.5 PR." I don't know what that stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to page 1, please, of that very document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we are short of time and have no time to analyse all of this, but you provided certain answers during cross-examination. Please look at item 2. What is mentioned here is the clean-up of Mojmilo, Sokolovic Kolonija, Dobrinja, and so on and so forth. During the war, who was at Mojmilo, Sokolovic Kolonija, Dobrinja, Butmir? Who controlled those locations? Let's start with Mojmilo and Sokolovic Kolonija. It says "mop-up" or "cleanse." Who held positions throughout the war there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war those positions were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 2 again. In item 5.1 there is mention of Mojmilo again; Sokolovic Kolonija as well. "Mop-up," it is a rather clear word in terms of its meaning in our language. Once you assumed your positions in the trenches, did you know then, or did you perhaps learn later, about the things mentioned here and who controlled those locations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only reiterate my previous answer, which is that the whole territory mentioned here was in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us move to page -- to document 770.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look. As you've seen already, there is the word "order" in that document, and please look at item 1. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The so-far TO units of the Serbian Defence Forces of Serbian Republic of BH restructure in larger groups and form them according to the following plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Subparagraph (e), therefore, paragraph 1(e), could you read that out loud as well, please. It begins with "Rajlovac ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Read it out.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rajlovac TO Brigade should be formed from the territory of Semizovac and Rajlovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When we go back to paragraph 1, what can we see? What is stressed there? I don't want to lead you, but you can read it again for yourself. What type of forces are mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence forces, the TO forces. The sentence says: "The so-far TO units of the Serbian Defence Forces of Serbian Republic of BH restructure in larger groups and form them according to the following plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, who got organised first to get that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina organised themselves first. That's why our forces are referred to as defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does "TO" mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive any interpretation, but I guess it is not important any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I said was that that concludes your evidence. The Chamber thanks you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If I may have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a procedural matter that Ms. Isailovic would like to address to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to ask for protective measures for this witness. We're talking about the witness T-47. He should be granted protective measures which were given to him in the Galic case already, and according to your decision you have granted him protective measures as well. So I would just like to remind the Chamber that he is going to have a pseudonym and his voice will be distorted as well -- rather, his face will be distorted. But, Your Honour, we met with the witness when he arrived in The Hague. Mr. T-47 requested of us to ask the Chamber to lift these measures because he does not object to testify in open session. So he will testify under his own name, and we are presenting an oral motion that these protective measures be lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber welcomes that. Trials are meant to be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. My colleague already explained. So the next witness is Kovacevic -- oh, Samardzic, Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness enters, it doesn't really have anything to do with him, before the trial began -- actually, I wanted to ask you even today that T-23 be the next witness to be heard. He's also protected -- or, rather, T-31. Could he be the next one instead of T-23, because that witness has urgent personal matters to attend to and he would like to finish as soon as possible with giving evidence. And I've already discussed this with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see no objection to that. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could I just make sure that -- because I see the screen is still down in front of me, are all protective measures being waived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding. That was what was requested. So would the screen be lifted, please. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will start my examination-in-chief. We have already met, so let's not go into that over here. Even before you entered the courtroom, I told you, because you're a rather temperamental man, that you should speak as slowly as possible, that you should wait until the typing stops, the typing of the transcript, that is. And I hope it's going to be easy for you to adjust since you were already a witness here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges -- can you tell the Judges what your name is, first and last name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Zoran Samardzic is my name. I was born on the 31st of March, 1953, in Nevesinje, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Sarajevo, in Hadzici, in the municipality of Sarajevo, that's where you've been living since 1964.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I came from Nevesinje in 1964 to Hadzici with my parents and my brother. That's where I went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Please. So elementary school, secondary school for catering and your training for a higher degree in catering, all of that took place in Sarajevo in 1970. That's when you finished.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Immediately after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: -- if you let me continue. As soon as I finished school, I was invited to take up a job as a caterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. I wanted to put a direct question to you about your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army; that you completed that immediately after your schooling in 1972 and 1973.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us where it was that you worked until the conflict broke out, if you can explain that in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I can. When I returned from the former army, the JNA, in 1973, as we've already said, I got a job at the Hadzici Remontni Zavod, overhaul facility, as the head of the cafeteria and a coffee corner. Up to the war in 1992, I worked there all the time as a caterer and cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just explain something lest there be any misunderstanding, although I informed the Prosecutor about this. Our investigator, when he took your details and talked to you, he noted down that you were a technician at the Zavod. Could you explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, loud and clear. I was appointed head of the cafeteria. I was called "tehnicki rukovaoc," not "tehnicki rukovodilac." It's technical handler. And I often complained about that, because it's not that I handled a machine or something. So it just had to do with my appointment. But actually, I am a caterer, highly qualified at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how many years did you spend working there as a caterer providing food to employees at this facility from the moment when you took that job?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately 19, 20 years, from 1973 to 1992. So in 1992 -- may I say this? May I say what it was that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. In this facility, who were the employees? Who worked there? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Remontni Zavod employed almost 2.000 persons, different types of workers. There were a few technical persons who were at a higher level like me. These were people who had degrees in electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, and then they took a commission as officers. Actually, they were the foremen and they worked in these plants just like the workers did. They wore blue coats just like the workers did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the cafeteria, the restaurant, you made sure that these people were fed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I guess my question was a bit too direct. Maybe it wasn't appropriate, this question. Actually, I put a leading question, Your Honours, but I don't think that this constitutes major abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is it that you took care of over all of those 19 years?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I took care of is providing food to the people there and to have normal life and work there in the cafeteria and the restaurant, and to make sure that everything was provided for hot meals for the employees at the Zavod.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these engineers with higher education, what did they organise on the premises where you worked? What was it that they were repairing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Since this was a factory of the land forces of the army of the former Yugoslavia, part of the weaponry from the former units of the Yugoslav People's Army came there for being repaired or overhauled, and these high-ranking people dealt with that, too; of course, with the repairmen as well. So they were called technical personnel, like me. I was also, like they, a civilian working in the armed forces. However, as opposed to myself, they were higher ranking, technical military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any officers there who at the time took care about the organisation of the military from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No, never, because this was a factory that was solely there for the purpose of repairing and overhauling and maintaining equipment. We just had mechanical and electrical engineering people who were promoted to technical ranks. No way did they -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who financed the work of these people? Who paid their salaries? Under whose control was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The Zavod was a company based on principles of acquiring and distributing income, and in terms of some fields of cooperation, we were responsible to the Ministry of Defence of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that precise reply. I don't have a convenient map so that you could indicate this directly, so I will be compelled, well, provided that you maintain contact with the microphone, that you somehow turn around and show where the Remontni Zavod is, where Hadzici is, where this institution was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it assists Mr. Tapuskovic at all, I have a convenient map, in fact a cut-out, that he may want to upload on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, because we've been through this exercise before, and I'm afraid it requires a kind of contortion that most of the witnesses are not capable of achieving.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could invite either of the Defence counsel, if we could have just a brief moment to have a look at these to see whether they choose to use them. They may not. But certainly visually it's going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please pass them over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In all honesty, I hadn't checked that book recently, but I suspect these are going to be in far more detail and we'll be able to see them on our monitors. The Defence may not want to use them, but at least I make the offer. If I may look at the map again, Mr. Court Officer, we may be able to get it up on the ELMO -- sorry, on e-court. It's not yet uploaded. It will have to go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it. This is where Hadzici is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can you explain to the Judges what Hadzici was before the conflict broke out. Could you please explain that so that it is clear who it was that this belonged to and what happened later. However, in order to be able to talk about what was there later, what was Hadzici in terms of its position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Hadzici was Sarajevo, just like Ilidza was Sarajevo; Dobrinja, Nedzarici, Grbavica. That is to say, all of that was an integral part of Sarajevo. Somebody belonged to the inner city of Sarajevo. We were a bit further away, but we made up Sarajevo. Up until the moment when the armies of -- BH army took Mojmilo, Stupsko Brdo, Zuc, there was an automatic division of the town into two parts. I, as a local Sarajevo man, all of a sudden felt as if I were not a man of Sarajevo and they were. So do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So when Sarajevo -- actually, when these things happened, you explained just now -- I don't want to dwell on that now, but we will come to that again, I mean, to what you were talking about just now. I'm now interested in hearing what it was that was going on in this factory where you worked, among the people you lived with all those years. What was going on in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Hadzici itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: All right. Hadzici itself, as a town, and my factory, Remontni Zavod, lived in peace up until 1992. The 14th of February, 1992, when only Muslims, ethnic Muslims, responded to the referendum, there was some unrest. There were tensions and separation in terms of groups. As I told you, I was head of the restaurant and therefore I had the opportunity of seeing, because I walked through the restaurant with the best of intentions of meeting people, seeing whether they were pleased with the food and whether everything was all right. Smaller groups were made up. As soon as I would walk up to a table of ethnic Muslims who were having breakfast, they would fall silent. I'd walk away and then they'd start whispering again. What it was they were talking about, I don't know. However, that in itself caused a certain feeling of distrust on my part. I did not know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in February?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: What happened in March and April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Already in March and April the media and the TV showed certain events in Sijekovac and the plight of civilians there, and therefore this contributed to tensions increasing in the Zavod, and it culminated sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in May? Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I remember it as clearly as it is today. It was the 8th of May, around noon. Members of the Muslim ethnic community left the Zavod. Only 200 or 300 Serbs remained who were taken by surprise. They were completely puzzled about what was happening. No one understood anything until the early evening hours. At around 1930, shooting started targeting the Zavod and Hadzici from the village of Dupovci. I can show you on the map. This is Dupovci. So fire was opened at the Zavod without any reason whatsoever. We were completely surprised. And I said a minute ago, since my factory was repairing the weapons for the former Yugoslav army, the people who remained behind, we took rifles - some of them were in working order, some were not - and we responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was the type of weapons that were in the factory? You already said that these were broken weapons. And later on I'm going to ask you more about this. In the subsequent events, were there any weaponry in working order that happened to be there in the repair shop? Were there any working weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since my working place was nearby, I saw that there were two tanks, two Pragas, which are 30-millimetre guns. In order to avoid any confusion, this is not a cannon, 30 millimetre. And two BRDM, and what it stands for, I have no idea at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the rest that was on the premises of the Zavod, what was the condition of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It was not functioning, except for part of light weapons, that is to say, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened? That was on the 8th of May. Do you recall any of the days that came after that date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Soon thereafter, on the 12th of May, i.e., four days after the attack on the Zavod, the entire Hadzici was attacked. A large-scale offensive was launched from the direction of Pazarici towards the city and the Remontni Zavod and the surrounding villages. So that was on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you show us approximately where Pazarici is? Can it be seen on the map? And if you can't see it, tell us approximately where it is. In that direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness also mentioned that this was in the direction of Gradac. This will facilitate our work later so that we know exactly where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the days that followed? This was on the 12th of May. What happened with the officers who were the employees, like you, and were not proper military officers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Already on the 15th of May, these officers, the so-called technical military personnel, and their families left Hadzici and Sarajevo. There were Serbs, Macedonians, and Croats among them, so each one of them exercised their right to return to their respective states. Only we remained with one officer and a lieutenant colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the details of the person he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you are speaking too fast. You said something about the lieutenant colonel which the interpreter did not hear. Would you please repeat it. Yes, repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that after they left Hadzici and Zavod in Sarajevo by these officers, only one of them remained. This man was from Banja Luka in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His name was Stevan Radivojesa, a mechanical engineer. He was the only one among the officers, if I may call them that, who stayed with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, we are not going to be able to explain anything to the Judges unless both you and I make our effort to rein in our temper and speak more slowly. Nothing will be recorded in the transcript. Let us try and speak at this pace, please. So what happened with these officers' families?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Their families left together with them. They left Hadzici and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you mentioned -- did you say on what date that took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The 15th of May. The 15th of May, 1992, that is to say, immediately after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any news about what was happening elsewhere, in other municipalities of Sarajevo? Hadzici is one municipality. Did you know what was going on in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I have certain information that there was shooting at Ilidza as well; also Nedzarici, Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about what was happening in the part of Sarajevo called Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were casualties there as well, that Pofalici was simply cleansed. The people who managed to escape, so to say, saved their lives, and those who couldn't escape were killed. A huge number of people were killed, civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton has a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, two points, actually, Your Honour, if I may, the first being that there was absolutely no mention of the events on Pofalici in the 65 ter summary from this witness, and the second being that this question and answer regarding Pofalici are completely without foundation. And frankly, Your Honour, I fail to see the relevance of events in Pofalici to events in Hadzici, which is what I understood from the 65 ter summary was going to be the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us ask Mr. Tapuskovic to answer that. Firstly, the 65 ter summary not mentioning Pofalici, but to me more important, what is the relevance of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't mention in any summary all the places in Sarajevo. Otherwise, the whole summary would just be made up of the list of names of municipalities in Sarajevo. And there is not a single witness for whom I said that I do not want to question about his personal status and condition and that of the area where he or she was living when the conflict broke out. This will be very helpful for your understanding of the overall situation, in order to enable the witness to speak about everything that is contained in the summary, and that is about combat activities, his or her participation, what he or she experienced, et cetera. And in this case, it refers only to Hadzici. He never left Hadzici. Hadzici is a municipality in Sarajevo that shared the destiny of the rest of Sarajevo. He said once Mojmilo and Stup were captured, he finally and suddenly -- correction, suddenly found himself in a town which was not called Sarajevo any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We rule that the question should not be asked on the basis that we are not satisfied about its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Witness, I will refrain to the issues that you personally experienced, and that is precisely what I want to hear from you. After all of this, you said under what circumstances you took up arms. Tell us briefly what happened later in the month that followed, May, and what you said.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So after the 15th of May, as I already said, when the officers, the technical staff and their families left the Zavod, on the 25th of May there was another fierce offensive. We again managed to defend ourselves, to consolidate our ranks. We set up a defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you show us on the map where this defence line was and -- first of all, let's see where the defence line was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: This red line, is that what you mean? This is immediately in the village of Dupovci that I mentioned a few minutes ago. When we entered and set up the line, the line ran through certain houses even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This may help Mr. Tapuskovic, but this map, this cut-out, is available on e-court now with ter number 02792D. That would allow the witness to mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We should then have that map displayed. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, only I'm not sure whether we can plot any markings on this. And I agree, Your Honours, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 02792D. If you could try to call that up in e-court. And there we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the line where you took up position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you have just said that you were first fired at on the 8th of May from Dupovci. Can you put a circle around that location, i.e., Dupovci.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And mark it with the letter D.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before you took up the line that you drew, what did you find in Dupovci?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In the houses, in the cellars, small windows were covered with blankets and other soft stuff. So we were under the impression that these were loopholes. Each house was connected to the next one with communicating trenches. Even further, people lifted floors from their rooms and dug tunnels under the ground in order to connect themselves with the next house. We found stocks of milk, chocolate, bandages, olive-drab sweaters with a red and black and yellow flag on the sleeves, which is the German flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you take positions on the line? Was it here or somewhere else so that we cannot see it in the map? Can you just point the direction on the map from Dupovci.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I would like to apologise to the Trial Chamber. I'm very bad with reading and handling maps. I used to work in the logistics. I was a cook. I know that the line was here, but I'm not sure whether I will be able to put the correct line on the map. This is where my fellow combatants were, and I was in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the nearest location to where your position was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: A transformer station was situated between the Remontni Zavod and Dupovci. This was at the very gate to the Zavod. This was a kind of power plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you on the separation line?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: After the 25th of May and the offensive that I mentioned earlier, I was transferred to the separation line, to the village of Kasatici at the foot of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, we have been dealing with this map. Could you tell us now what the name of this place was where you were at the positions, well, nearby?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The village of Dupovci. That is not far away from the Zavod.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon. You've already explained that. But then when you came to the positions, the separation line, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The village of Kasatici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you draw an arrow from Dupovci towards the place where you were, because Kasatici cannot be seen here.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kasatici cannot be seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw an arrow from Dupovci to the place where Kasatici was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it assists again, I have another map what has Kasatici on it, and we could advise the Trial Chamber, I think momentarily, of the ter number. The numbers are just getting uploaded into e-court at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the cooperation of the Prosecution is indeed commendable. Let's have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we upload it, perhaps I can just ask the court officer to show this to Mr. Tapuskovic to see if he's interested in using this map. And Kasatici is on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm going to lose quite a bit of time. I just wanted to ask the witness to show whether it's south or east in relation to Dupovci. I just want him to draw an arrow where it is, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can you just indicate with an arrow whether it's east or south of Dupovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing? Then I will have to use what the Prosecutor proposed. I thank the Prosecutor. I believed that he could tell the cardinal points, but -- well, it's not of such decisive importance now. Could this map be kept now for the time being. I think that I have to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, when you were at these lines, front lines, what was the distance between your line, the line where you were, and the line of the other side? What was the distance there of those positions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Not more than 500 metres, which is to say that we were 500 metres away from the enemy line, if I can call it that. From the centre of Hadzici, we were 2 kilometres away, and they were facing Pazarici. So 8 to 9 kilometres to the civilian population; that is to say, there were absolutely no civilians there, only the military in trenches, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you were on the other side in the trenches. Where were you at the positions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Kasatici, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But where were you? In a house or what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was in a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when there was combat activity, can you describe what it was like at the separation line. How did you operate as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: We had light infantry weapons, automatic rifles, and that is what we used to fight. We had support for a while of those two tanks that I mentioned at the outset and those two Pragas, so only light of infantry weapons. And we had these tanks as support and those two Pragas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've already explained what was there at the Zavod where you were. And what was in Pazarici before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In Pazarici, that is where a barracks was located. I'd lived there for so many years and I did not realise this was barracks for training artillerymen. And in 1992, it just so happened an artillery regiment was transferred there from Zadar, also from the artillery centre. This barracks was under total blockade up until the 21st of May, 1992, I think, when the barracks were deblocked and when the cadets who were there training were taken on two buses of the Zavod, the overhaul facility, to a safe place. And I don't know where that was. These two buses were driven by my two colleagues Metis Dobrica and Tesic Zivko, who also worked at the Zavod. These same people told me that in these barracks, because this was a centre for training artillerymen, there was a lot of heavy weaponry that was left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you had support from these two tanks and these heavy weapons. What did this activity look like? You said that you had guns, rifles, and this support from heavy weapons. In relation to you, where was this directed, then, and where was this falling, as for your forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, these tanks were firing at the front lines in front of us, their trenches. They were supporting us, and they were trying all the time to break through our line, all the time, from day to day almost. So we had fierce fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for your lines where you were, how far away was Pazarici? How far away were the first civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Eight to 10 kilometres. Around 9 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the army that was in the trenches in front of you? Did they have support, artillery support, as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. From this deblockaded barracks, they had all the equipment that had been left there. They took this. They repaired whatever there was, but there were quite a few heavy calibres there; 152-millimetre howitzers, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, when they would fire, where would this fall, that is to say, what had been fired from these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It hardly ever fell on our lines. It fell in the very heart of the urban area of Hadzici; that is to say, it was the civilian population that was being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, until when did you stay at the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I stayed all the way up to February 1993. That is when conditions were created for the organised feeding of the army, and then I was transferred to head the military mess, if I can call it that, and that is where I stayed until the end of the war. As for 1993, there was lots of fighting and many shells fell on the urban area of Hadzici. At one point in time, the 13th of April, a fateful moment for me, I was visiting a friend who, on that day at 11.00 in the morning, got hit in the street. I found him in all bandages. And then when I returned to my apartment, I found my child dead and his colleague, Srdjan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness take a minute to compose himself. Perhaps a glass of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go on, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, I have to ask you about this. You have to tell the Judges what it was that happened, what you saw, and whether anybody else was a victim in addition to your child.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: My only child, Sasa, 13 years old he was, he got killed, and his colleague --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you really need the details of this, Mr. Tapuskovic? I can't see that you really need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need this. I even have the photographs; I'm not going to show them. But now when -- I mean, heaven forbid, it never crossed my mind. I'm not asking -- I mean, I don't want to play with other people's feelings. I certainly don't want to do that. But this witness lost his only son, and I asked him whether somebody else was a victim there in addition to his only son. Now, if that is irrelevant, well, I understand His Honour Judge Harhoff not to have this kind of thing discussed, but I don't understand. I mean, I'm asking the witness to give us at least basic information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there another victim apart from your son? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another boy, Srdjan Zuza. He was 11 years old. I found them both in pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How old was your son?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Thirteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was only the other day that I received this document which only refers to the date of death of this boy, his son. The document is DD003762. What matters is the date that coincides with the date when his son lost his life. It's not been translated, but I would like it to be shown to you that this is a death certificate, the 13th of April, 1993. If that can be admitted into evidence, because it is our document DD003762.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position from the outset has been that there was an armed conflict and in fact we have called evidence of the suffering of the Serbian population in and around Sarajevo as part of the Prosecution case. I'm not here to make a parent who's lost his son suffer any further. If Mr. Tapuskovic feels he needs to put these documents into evidence, of course I have no objection. But I don't see how it's germane to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we think it is only of marginal relevance. We admit it, but we encourage you to move on from this topic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document ID DD003762 will be admitted as D229.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the map please be given a number. An exhibit number for the map. Can it be a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours will admit the map as D230.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I can also ask him is that relevant or perhaps is that irrelevant as well. At that time, I mean before we move on to 1994, at that time, as a result of these military activities, were there other civilian casualties or not? Or is this irrelevant as well? Should I simply not ask him about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993 there were also casualties in flats. For example, in a flat in the city -- in the centre of the town of Hadzici, the mother of a friend of mine was killed while she was having a coffee in her first-floor apartment. A shell came from Igman, fell on the parking lot, and killed her in her flat. Her name was Ruzica Roncevic Ruza. It also killed my neighbour, Mrs. Savka Sarenac. She was standing on the balcony in my building. That was also in 1993. After 1993, until 1994 there was a truce for longer periods. There was sporadic fire, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993 or 1994, what was the situation like -- well, let's begin with 1994. What was the situation with food supplies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Since I was the manager of the mess, Serbia imposed sanctions and it was extremely difficult to find raw materials for the kitchen and for preparing food for the troops. It was difficult. I remember in 1994, in winter, the beginning of winter, all heavy weaponry around Sarajevo was withdrawn. What ensued was a period of cease-fire with intermittent fire and constant shelling of the centre of Hadzici. Not so intensive, but it was on a daily basis. Every day at least ten shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic was appointed commander of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was in August of 1994, the end of August. And after that, until 1995 - excuse me - there was a sort of truce. But I always have to emphasise, even during these periods of cease-fire, there was fierce fire. I remember clearly seeing from my window of my flat in October 1994 Nevena Sakota was killed in the middle of the street. She was a 19-year-old girl. Also killed was Biljana Krunic, another young girl. She was 18 or 19. One of my employees, Slavko Bujak - and I saw it with my own eyes - lost his leg in those days and he died less than a year later. Sometime in the beginning of November 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton is on her feet. We must hear her.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my extreme sympathies to the victims, but as I've already indicated, we've even called this evidence as part of the Prosecution case. Incidents in Hadzici town are nowhere within the indictment against this accused and I would question the relevance of this testimony at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You make the point, then, Ms. Edgerton, that in terms of the geographic compass of the indictment, Hadzici is outside that area. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's not a single incident on the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness explained very well that Hadzici was part of Sarajevo, that Hadzici was part of Sarajevo, that Hadzici ceased to be part of Sarajevo after one army occupied Stupsko Brdo and Mojmilo hill and all those other hills east of Hadzici. Hadzici, Ilijas, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, Grbavica, all of that is Sarajevo, just like Zuc and Hum are and all other places. I'm going to ask the witness now to tell us what happened in November, what he knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I have not yet ruled. You can't ask the witness anything. You have to wait for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean to put the question. However, these events are part of what was happening in the relevant period concerning the responsibility of Dragomir Milosevic and his zone of responsibility, that is to say, the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that Hadzici ceased to be part of Sarajevo after one army occupied Stupsko Brdo, Mojmilo hill, et cetera. Which army was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That happened only in the minds of certain people, that Hadzici, Rajlovac, Ilijas, could cease to be Sarajevo. It's all Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer the question -- two questions, or, rather, two parts to the question: Which army occupied the parts of Mojmilo, and what time was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied Mojmilo, Stupsko Brdo, and thereby cut Sarajevo in two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, in May and June, all of this happened, and that is how it remained until the end of the war. Mojmilo and Stupsko Brdo; that is to say, the separation lines cut the city of Sarajevo into two parts. Hadzici, Rajlovac, Vogosca, Ilijas, were all the places in the zone of responsibility of the SRK, and they're all part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only to stipulate that it's the Prosecution's position that the VRS held Stup. That's my only clarification. Your Honour, I think we're talking about what my -- with respect, my friend is talking about a division which may have happened in the minds of certain people, as he said. Sarajevo never ceased to exist as a city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, on your own submission, Hadzici ceased to be part of Sarajevo well before the indictment period, for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, my learned friend says that the VRS was holding Stup. The army of Republika Srpska never held Stup. Throughout the whole conflict it was held by the BH army. Hadzici can never cease to be part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us how the events in Hadzici become relevant to the core of the charges, which is the siege of Sarajevo, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to repeat. Hadzici never ceased to be part of Sarajevo. For centuries, or at least for 100 years, it was part of Sarajevo, and I already explained under what circumstances. It was not in the inner part of Sarajevo, although the residents of Sarajevo believed it to be part of the core of Sarajevo. There can be no Sarajevo without Hadzici, without Ilijas, or any other place. This is how it was and this is how it is going to remain. At any rate, in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, you haven't answered the question that I asked, which was to illustrate how the events in Hadzici become relevant to the core of the indictment which is concerned with the siege of Sarajevo, the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the issue. Who was under siege, actually? Who was under siege and where? Was Grbavica under siege? Was Nedzarici under siege? It is up to you to give the final answer, because the Defence thinks that Grbavica was under siege, that Nedzarici was under siege, that Dobrinja was under siege, and that maybe under the worst siege was Hadzici. This word "siege" means nothing under these specific circumstances. Everybody was under siege at the time, especially after the tunnel became operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, just for clarification, do you remember this map that we were given in the beginning of the trial? Sorry. Do you remember -- do you have this map with you? Because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's number 10 map used by Mrs. Ewa Tabeau. I think we should look at that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is map 2 in this binder. Yes. Let me, just for clarity, ask you: Is it, in your opinion, the case that this trial is about everything and anything that happened within the thick purple line, which includes Hadzici to the west, Trnovo to the south, Pale to the east, and Ilijas to the north? In other words, this entire area here. Is that, in your view, encompassed by the indictment? Let me show you also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, quite certainly this whole area in the zone of responsibility of the SRK, and particularly what used to be Sarajevo - Ilidza, Hadzici, Novo Sarajevo - and everything else constitutes Sarajevo. And it is completely unclear who encircled whom. If we were to look at individual parts, as we did in the course of this trial, especially after the tunnel became operational and particularly depending on how you are going to assess who had dominant positions on the hill, if we're going to separate this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then just use the indictment to support your point. What is the relevant area as alleged in the indictment? Can you help us with that? I'm trying to find it. Most of the references are simply to Sarajevo. Many references to the civilian population of Sarajevo. For example, paragraph 24 alleges that the Serb forces conducted a campaign of artillery, et cetera, and modified air bomb shelling onto the civilian areas of Sarajevo and its civilian population. If we look at the terror count, again, reference to the civilian areas of Sarajevo and the civilian population. So the question is: What do we mean by "Sarajevo"? I have made up my mind. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We rule the question to be admissible -- permissible. We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you've already said what happened by the end of 1994. What was the period after that like, for example, concerning food, the end of 1994 and then 1995? Let us try to wrap things up, if we can.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: As I've already stated, sanctions were imposed, and it was increasingly difficult to buy certain things needed to provide meals for the army. And the rumour had it, although I wasn't present, although I've lived there my whole life, that there was a tunnel at Dobrinja that was used in late 1994 and 1995. There was a large-scale offensive in October 1994 lasting until December that year. In the lull that ensued in 1995, they dug out that tunnel and it was used exclusively by the ABiH in order to move their troops to Igman and some other elevations that were nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you tell the Judges how come you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I heard that from my friends and co-fighters, because they could move about, although it was very risky since there was shooting all the time. I spoke to some of those people who managed to see that the tunnel was in existence. It was shown on TV, although I cannot recall exactly when. They used the tunnel to move people and some war equipment and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: What was the situation like by the end of December and the months following that in Hadzici and in your area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: When I talk about Hadzici, I keep thinking about Sarajevo because I was an inhabitant of that city. There was a cease-fire which lasted all the way until June 1995. I think it was the 15th of June when there was an all-out offensive from all front lines, from all sides, against the centre of Sarajevo and Ilijas and Grbavica, everything that comprised Sarajevo. There was an all-out offensive. Until early June there were no major incidents. There was a cease-fire in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties at that time? You needn't go into any names or similar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Certainly there were casualties and victims, as in any other clash or conflict. There must have been some. I know for sure that in Hadzici, throughout the war, over 220 civilians were killed and a number of troops. I don't know their exact number, but there were over 220 civilians killed. The offensive lasted until -- almost until the Dayton Accords were concluded. Even after the signing of the accords there were provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what happened with the people who were there, who stayed there throughout the conflict? What happened after the Dayton Accords with Hadzici, Ilidza, Vogosca, and the people who lived there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I left Hadzici in 1996, in late February, and I never returned. I spent my entire life there. I grew up there, went to school and worked, and suffered the tragedy I mentioned. I don't want to go back to it. The entire population of Hadzici left. People went different ways. I live in Trnovo, which is a part of the municipality of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours, while I check my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now based on some of the things you've testified about today, and if you don't understand anything or if I'm unclear at all, please say. You've testified today about - on page 22 of your testimony - the location of Hadzici, and I'd like you to tell us, if you could give us an estimate of how far in kilometres the town is from the urban area of Sarajevo, say, from the town centre until Marin Dvor, as the crow flies, let's say.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that Marin Dvor or my building is exactly 21 kilometres by road, which means probably half of it, as the crow flies. I'd say 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Twenty-one kilometres by road and 10, as the crow flies. Now, what was the ethnic composition of Hadzici municipality, as far as you know? And here I speak about the municipality and not the town itself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The urban part, the town, was mixed; 50 per cent -- excuse me. There were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, but the Muslims prevailed in the municipality since they usually populated the villages around. I would say that there was 70 per cent Muslims in the municipality while the rest were Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your testimony you had lived in peace as a community up until 1992, but in fact the elected municipal authorities had actually collapsed in October 1991, hadn't they? There was no assembly, no municipality assembly, after that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: There was no municipal assembly, but there were some parties in power. There was the SDS, the SDA, the HDZ. I don't know what I would call that situation. Things weren't clear. There was no municipal president or president of the assembly. I don't know what the authorities functioned like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, the Serbian municipality of Hadzici was proclaimed as early as April 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In April 1992? Well, I think so, yes, because the police had divided by then. I don't know whether it took place in March or April. But I think I already said that. It was a nightmare, a general chaos. I don't know how the municipality functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And road links between Sarajevo and Hadzici were actually blocked from the very beginning of April 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It is correct. But in 1992, in March and April, there were check-points with the reserve police force, and those people were Muslims. The Serbs were in the town itself. I don't know what they controlled in the inner town. But as for the perimeter, say, the entrance to Hadzici, I myself was several times stopped by policemen and they searched me and the vehicle as well as the colleagues who were with me. I couldn't understand why, because up until that time things were peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They were in the town -- the Serbs were in the town as a separate police force; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just one comment that seems to be useful. Page 47 of the transcript, lines 6 and 7, maybe the question should be asked again, because Mr. Samardzic talked about the police. He said that he was searched by the police. This is what he said. That was not written down in the transcript. He said that it was -- the people who searched him were his classmates or people with whom he went to school. He said those were people with whom he went to school when he was a child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, would you just repeat that part of your evidence relating to the search.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. For example, I went to Ilidza in Sarajevo. I had relatives there and friends. When returning home, I was greatly surprised, because when I tried to enter the town, the police stopped me. I pulled over. They were in uniform. They asked me to open the trunk. And these people used to go to school with me. Some of them were still bachelors, but some were already married by that time. For example, Adis Dzankic was one of them. Perhaps I can say this as well: I asked his mother Adisa where Adis was, because by that time I had realised that he had been drafted by the Muslim police. She said he was there. And I said, "Well, I see him every day. He goes out with a rifle and returns without it." And the lady was stunned. They were behaving strangely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the Serbian police in the town centre, they were operating in a separate building, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What can you tell us, Mr. Samardzic, about an ultimatum that was issued by the SDS to the Muslims of Hadzici on 7th May to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any ultimatums. What I do know, though, is that the Muslim inhabitants had left the town earlier, by end of April. I saw them myself from Zavod. A saw a woman with two children and an old man. They were on an ox cart moving towards a forest on an elevation. They had packs on the cart. After the first clashes broke out, after early May when we entered those villages, the houses there were full. They didn't take much with them. They only pulled out the infirm and the children. There was no ultimatum on the Serb side. It was impossible how the villages were empty. They left willingly, leaving their houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, are you saying that, to the best of your knowledge, there was no ultimatum by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I know that many people -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Samardzic, also on the 7th of May, Serb army reservists and Serb policemen entered the municipality building in Hadzici, evicted the staff and locked the building, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The 7th of May? I really don't know, believe me that, or I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And around that time, the Serb police, in front of the building that they occupied, took a weapon, an anti-aircraft gun, and placed it in front of their police station, aiming it outward, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: A gun, you say? I don't understand. What gun?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: An anti-aircraft gun, Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It could have only been a Browning. It is a 12.7-millimetre gun. I wouldn't call that a gun. I wouldn't call it a cannon. There were no big cannons at first. When shells start flying about, you don't know where they're coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take from your answer, then, that there was a weapon which was placed in front of the Serb police station in Hadzici before the 8th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: If I said that there was a weapon, I didn't say it was mounted. Maybe there was something of that calibre, but all I'm saying is that there was no cannon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've given evidence that shooting in and around the town centre started on 8th of May, 1992, at around 7.30. Now, Mr. Samardzic, isn't it a fact that following this incident non-Serbs from the town of Hadzici were progressively moved from their homes and incarcerated in detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. All I know is that a part of the population left willingly towards Pazarici. No one was driving them away, I swear on that. Many Muslims stayed behind with us in the buildings since they were married to Serbs. They weren't loyal to the Serb side, but they stayed in their houses, and later they worked in different aspects of civilian protection, for example, food supply. My colleague, Ismet Nizic, was a waiter - he's died in the meantime - and he worked on the distribution of food to the Serbs and Muslims. There was no terror. No one forced anyone out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Once again, I would like to mention that on the transcript, page 50, line 11, I read on the transcript "were married with Serbs," but -- and I hear very -- I heard the witness, I heard what the witness said, but I never heard the witness mention that somebody was married to the Serbs. He used the word "mixed marriages," but he didn't say that somebody was married, "ozenjen," or "udat," with a Serb. So he talked about mix marriages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The sentence really should have read, then: "Many stayed behind with us in the buildings since there were mixed marriages"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, because the witness did not mention the word about being married to someone. The witness did not say Bosnians were married to Serbs, or he didn't say that a Swiss person was married to a person of the another nationality. The witness did not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We got the point. You should bear in mind, Ms. Isailovic, that the transcript is routinely corrected, so that unless you see something which you consider is going to be relevant to the examination, to your examination, or the cross-examination, I would encourage you to leave it alone and to take it up only if you think it is going to become vital to the rest of the examination of the witness, or cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to reiterate that I intervene only when I believe that something will become important afterwards, not only for redirect, the redirect procedure, but also I only intervene when I think that it will stay written down and that perhaps can affect our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Samardzic, you've said that you don't know about ethnic cleansing, yet you've talked about a large number of non-Serbs leaving the municipality willingly. Mr. Samardzic, I put to you that those non-Serbs who remained in Hadzici were --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness never used the term "ethnic cleansing," not once. I fail to understand how we have such a question now involving ethnic cleansing. This person worked in the catering industry. He never mentioned ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, when I asked you whether or not you were aware of the removal of non-Serbs in Hadzici town from their homes and their detention in facilities in the municipality, you said you don't know, but you noted that a number of non-Serb women and children left the municipality willingly. Now, my question to you is: Are you saying that you have no knowledge that the remaining non-Serbs in Hadzici town were removed from their homes and placed in detention facilities in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't think that happened. I really don't know. Most of my day went to produce and make food. I really don't know. But I can say again that no one tried to influence anyone concerning their decision whether they would stay or leave Hadzici. No one bothered anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've testified previously that you never left Hadzici, and what I'd like to ask you, sir, then, is where -- and you worked at the technical refitting plant until you were sent on the line. So, sir, where is the Hadzici sports centre in relation to the technical refitting plant?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The sports centre is further down below, towards Remontni Zavod. I was up there throughout the war where the kitchen was; therefore, I have no idea what was happening in the sports centre. From the kitchen I was moved up to the front line in Kasatici. I've explained that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's time for the break. We'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
